title: Capital letters count
idea: String comparison is case-sensitive: "Red" and "red" are NOT equal. Predict matches that differ only by capitalization.

exercises.prompt:
What is the value of this?

"Red" == "red"
exercises.explanation: A capital R and a lowercase r are different characters, so the words are not an exact match - False.

exercises.prompt: String comparison treats "YES" and "yes" as the same word.
exercises.explanation: No - comparison is case-sensitive. Different capitalization means a different word to the computer.
"Yes" (capital Y) does not equal "yes" (lowercase), so the else runs. Case matters.
Only identical spelling AND identical case gives True. "blue" matches "blue" exactly.

exercises.prompt: Why might checking only answer == "yes" miss some users?
options: Someone might type "Yes" or "YES", which do not match "yes"
exercises.explanation: People capitalize differently. An exact lowercase check misses "Yes" and "YES" - a real-world gotcha.

exercises.prompt: A safe way to accept several capitalizations of yes, using tools you know, is...
options: if answer == "yes" or answer == "Yes" or answer == "YES"
exercises.explanation: Joining the variants with 'or' accepts any of them. (Reviewing 'or' from the boolean unit.)
'or' is true when either variant matches, so both spellings are accepted.
No - the extra space makes them different. Exact match counts every character, including spaces.
"STOP" does not equal "stop" because of case, so the else prints "Unknown command".

options: Word comparison is exact - case and spaces must match too
exercises.explanation: The computer compares letter by letter, exactly. Plan for the capitalizations users might actually type.
